config.title: Race Condition Fix

intro.title: Race Condition Fix
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that fetches and displays user data from an API, learning how to fix a common race condition bug. You will understand how race conditions occur when multiple asynchronous requests can complete out of order, leading to incorrect data being displayed. The core programming concepts involved are managing state with the useState hook, performing side effects with the useEffect hook, and using cleanup functions to cancel outdated requests. You'll work with JavaScript's fetch API and React's built-in hooks to implement a solution that ensures only the latest request's data is shown, making your app more reliable and user-friendly.
intro.usecase: Race conditions frequently occur in React applications when multiple asynchronous operations compete to update the same state. This is common in search interfaces where rapid typing triggers multiple API calls, and later responses can overwrite earlier ones, displaying incorrect results. It also affects dashboard components that fetch real-time data from multiple sources, where stale data can replace fresh updates. Understanding race condition fixes ensures users see accurate, predictable information in critical interfaces like financial dashboards, e-commerce filters, and collaborative editing tools.

objectives: Implement a controlled component to manage user input and prevent conflicting state updates
Apply a loading state to disable interactions during asynchronous operations
Construct a cleanup function to abort pending requests when components unmount
Configure a unique request identifier to track and ignore outdated responses
Update component state conditionally based on the most recent request
Integrate error boundaries to handle failed requests without disrupting the UI
Manipulate the order of asynchronous operations to ensure predictable outcomes

steps.hint: Use async/await with Math.random() to generate a random delay. Remember to multiply by 2000 and add 1000 to get a range of 1000-3000 milliseconds.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a fetchData function that can be called later to simulate API requests with varying delays.
successCriteria: The component contains an async fetchData function that takes an id parameter, uses setTimeout with a random delay, and returns a string containing the id.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Implement useEffect with cleanup to fix race condition
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook inside your component that tracks the current request and includes a cleanup function using a boolean flag to prevent state updates from stale requests.
steps.hint: Create a useEffect with an empty dependency array. Inside it, define a boolean variable (like 'ignore') and set it to false. In the cleanup function (returned from useEffect), set that variable to true. Use this flag to conditionally update state only when the request is still relevant.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is implemented with a cleanup function that prevents race conditions by ignoring stale request results.
successCriteria: A useEffect hook is added with an empty dependency array, includes a boolean flag variable, and returns a cleanup function that sets the flag to true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your useEffect includes both the boolean flag variable and a cleanup function that sets it to true when the component unmounts or before the next effect runs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect implementation is missing key elements. Review the example: you need a boolean flag variable and a cleanup function that sets it to true to ignore stale requests.

steps.title: Update the fetch handler to use the cleanup flag
steps.instruction: In your component, update the handleFetch function to check if the component is still mounted before updating state by using a cleanup flag.
steps.hint: Inside handleFetch, create a local variable like 'isMounted' set to true. In the useEffect cleanup function, set it to false. Then in handleFetch, only update state if isMounted is true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleFetch function will now check the isMounted flag before updating state, preventing race conditions when components unmount during async operations.
successCriteria: handleFetch function includes a check for the isMounted flag before calling setData and setLoading
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check the isMounted flag in both places where you update state (setData and setLoading). The cleanup flag should prevent all state updates when the component is unmounted.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleFetch function doesn't properly check the cleanup flag. Remember to use the isMounted variable from the useEffect cleanup to conditionally update state only when the component is still mounted.
